top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) rewards a first-order, mature achievement: how technology and trade shift labour demand, wages and regional employment. It pairs the long-run skill supply-and-demand evidence (Katz) with transparent local-labour-market designs on import competition (Autor, Hanson). Autor links the two strands, so one citation worded around labour demand, wages and regional employment is coherent. It does not claim the task model as theory, which limits overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes. A decade or more of replication and critique has refined the magnitude, persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects but not the finding that adjustment is slow, concentrated and costly. The main costs are Dorn's exclusion under the three-name cap and the one-or-two-achievements question. If the committee narrowed the scope to import competition, Autor, Dorn and Hanson would be the defensible set. I rank P002 (Kiyotaki and Moore) second. It has the cleanest attribution and is nearly thirty years old, but it is mainly theoretical, its quantitative importance is established indirectly, and it sits next to the 2022 prize. Both awards are better than no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: No co-authorship or personal tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz, Kiyotaki or Moore is apparent from my profile. My research on capital-skill complementarity and inequality is adjacent to the skill-premium literature behind P001, which may bias me toward it. I am a frequent co-author of committee members Boppart and Hassler and a Stockholm University colleague of Teorell. None of these ties involves a credited name. They are disclosed, not adjudicated, and the ballot is completed.
